original_question: A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a dog bite. The patient was intoxicated and pulled the dog’s tail while it was eating. The dog belongs to his friend and is back at his friend’s house currently. Physical exam is notable for a dog bite on the patient’s right arm. The wound is irrigated and explored with no retained bodies found. A tetanus vaccination is administered. Which of the following is appropriate management of this patient?

base.stage_1: A 27-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a chief complaint of a dog bite to his right arm.
base.stage_2: The patient states he was intoxicated and pulled the dog's tail while it was eating, resulting in the bite. Examination reveals a single puncture wound on the right forearm. There is no active bleeding.
base.stage_3: The wound is irrigated and explored, with no foreign bodies identified. Tetanus vaccination is administered and up to date. Radiographs of the forearm show no evidence of fracture or retained teeth.
base.stage_4: The dog's owner confirms that the animal is fully vaccinated against rabies. Given the nature of the bite and the patient's presentation, prophylactic antibiotics are deemed necessary.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The patient reports the dog is his own and has been acting strangely for the past few days, becoming aggressive and agitated, which raises concern for possible rabies exposure.
